patient.name: Desmond Asante
patient.complaint: Central crushing chest pain at rest for 50 minutes, with sweating and nausea
background: Father had a myocardial infarction aged 55

diagnosis.exam: Expect a vignette of central crushing chest pain with sweating and nausea, then 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where you must place the patient on the UA / NSTEMI / STEMI spectrum, or spot a complication (new murmur, collapse, widespread ST elevation weeks later) or a mimic (costochondritis, cocaine).

points: 62M bus driver: **heavy, crushing central chest pain** at rest
Started watching TV; radiates to left jaw
Paramedics take him straight to resus

steps.lead: Textbook story: **central crushing** pain to the jaw, plus sweating and nausea. Autonomic features in a stem = think ACS.
Desmond has four risk factors: **smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history**. Examiners put these in the first line on purpose.

steps.q: Before any test results, what umbrella diagnosis best fits Desmond right now?
steps.r: Pain **at rest** with sweating and vomiting in a high-risk man = ACS until proven otherwise. Stable angina is exertional and settles with rest.

steps.lead: ACS is a spectrum. Where Desmond sits depends on two things: his **ECG** and his **troponin**.

steps.title: One plaque, three diagnoses
nodes: Partial occlusion, troponin normal: unstable angina
steps.caption: Same process; how much the thrombus occludes the artery and whether myocytes die decides the label.

steps.title: Placing a patient on the ACS spectrum
head: Unstable angina
NSTEMI
STEMI
rows: Normal or ischaemic changes (ST depression / T inversion)
Normal, ST depression or T-wave inversion

steps.q: The paramedic ECG shows **ST elevation in II, III and aVF**. Where is Desmond on the spectrum?
o: Cannot say until troponin is back
steps.r: ST elevation with the right story **is** a STEMI. Never wait for troponin to label or treat it.

steps.lead: As a diabetic he could have had a **silent MI** (breathless or nauseated only). A **new LBBB** would get the same STEMI pathway.

steps.title: Stable angina vs crescendo (unstable) angina
head: Stable angina
Crescendo / unstable angina
rows: Relieved by rest at first, then less so

steps.lead: No chest wall tenderness, no drugs. Rule out two mimics every time: **costochondritis** (tender to press) and **cocaine vasospasm** (young, party).
Pulse **48 bpm** + inferior STEMI = proximal RCA: risk of complete heart block, 3-fold 30-day mortality. Clear chest is good; crackles = cardiogenic shock.

steps.text: Complications by timing: **minutes–hours** = VF, heart block; **days** = VSR (new pansystolic murmur + heart failure, urgent echo); **weeks** = Dressler's (widespread ST elevation + PR depression).
Widespread ST elevation + PR depression weeks after MI = **Dressler's syndrome**, not a new STEMI. STEMI is territorial with reciprocal depression.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ECG), ECG lead-to-artery questions ('Which artery is most likely occluded?'), serial troponin timing, CK-MB for reinfarction and GRACE thresholds for angiography in NSTEMI.

points: 12-lead ECG recorded within **4 minutes** of arrival
Registrar reads it at the bedside

steps.q: What is the single most important first investigation in Desmond?
steps.r: ECG within **10 minutes** of arrival: it decides whether he goes straight to reperfusion. Troponin takes 2–3 hours to rise.

visual.title: Desmond's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL: inferior STEMI. Sinus bradycardia at 48 bpm, narrow QRS (no LBBB), V1–V6 normal.

steps.text: Find the ST **elevation** first, then the **reciprocal depression** opposite. The slow rate points to a proximal RCA.

steps.lead: ST elevation **II, III, aVF** with reciprocal I/aVL depression = inferior territory. Use this list for any ECG in a stem.

steps.title: ECG leads to culprit artery
nodes: II, III, aVF: inferior, right coronary artery
V7–V9 elevation with V1–V3 depression: posterior
steps.caption: Learn it as a map: lead groups look at walls, walls are fed by named arteries.

visual.title: Contrast: anterior STEMI
visual.caption: ST elevation V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior depression: anterior STEMI, LAD. If V5 and V6 were also elevated it would be anterolateral; I and aVL alone would be the circumflex.

steps.text: Same disease, different artery: now the **chest leads** carry the elevation and the inferior leads show reciprocal change.

steps.q: Which artery is most likely occluded in Desmond?
steps.r: Inferior leads = **RCA**. The RCA usually supplies the SA and AV nodes, so proximal occlusion risks bradycardia and complete heart block.

visual.title: Desmond's culprit artery
visual.caption: The right coronary artery supplies the inferior wall and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes. A proximal RCA block gives inferior STEMI with bradycardia and a risk of complete heart block.

steps.title: Initial bloods (0 hours)
steps.text: First troponin only mildly raised. CXR: normal heart size, clear lungs.
Other first tests: **FBC** (Hb, platelets before antithrombotics), **U&Es** (before contrast) and **CXR** (pulmonary oedema, wide mediastinum).

steps.lead: Pain began under an hour ago, so troponin is only mildly up. Diagnosis = **story + ECG + troponin**, and a repeat shows the rise.

steps.title: Repeat troponin (3 hours, after PCI)
steps.text: A sharp **rise** between samples confirms acute MI.

visual.title: Desmond's troponin
visual.caption: Barely raised at first, then a steep **rise**: acute MI. It stays high for days, so it cannot detect reinfarction (use CK-MB).

steps.text: In STEMI **never wait for troponin** to activate the cath lab. The ECG decides; troponin confirms later.

steps.q: On day 4 Desmond has new chest pain. His troponin is still high from the first event. Which marker best detects a reinfarction?
steps.r: Troponin stays raised for days. **CK-MB** falls quickly, so a re-elevation points to reinfarction.

steps.lead: Desmond is a STEMI, so no GRACE: straight to reperfusion. In NSTEMI the **GRACE score** decides how fast angiography happens.

steps.q: A different patient in the next bay has an NSTEMI with a GRACE score of 5.4%. What does this mean?
steps.r: GRACE **>3%** = coronary angiography within 72 hours. Thrombolysis is never used in NSTEMI.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the next most appropriate step in management?' after a stem that lists the drugs already given, so you must know the order: aspirin, MONA, second antiplatelet, anticoagulant, then primary PCI (or fibrinolysis if PCI is not timely). Also post-MI secondary prevention, eplerenone, Dressler's and DVLA rules.

steps.q: The ECG is being recorded. Which drug should Desmond receive immediately, even before the diagnosis is confirmed?
steps.r: **Aspirin 300 mg PO** straight away in every suspected ACS. Alteplase only if primary PCI cannot happen in time.

steps.lead: Sats 96%: **no oxygen**. Systolic 112: GTN is safe (avoid if <90). IV morphine + metoclopramide for pain and vomiting.

steps.title: Immediate drugs in suspected ACS
nodes: IV morphine + metoclopramide if severe pain

steps.q: Desmond is going for PCI and takes no anticoagulant. Which second antiplatelet fits the notes best?
steps.r: **Prasugrel 60 mg** if going for PCI and not anticoagulated. Clopidogrel if already on apixaban or warfarin.

steps.title: Choosing the second antiplatelet
head: Drug
Choose when
Watch out
rows: Already anticoagulated (apixaban, warfarin) or high bleeding risk

steps.lead: Onset 50 minutes ago, cath lab on site: PCI well within **120 minutes**. He goes for **primary PCI** via the radial artery.

steps.title: STEMI reperfusion decision
nodes: STEMI or new LBBB, onset within 12 hours
Yes: primary PCI with drug-eluting stent
Repeat ECG at 60–90 min: persistent ST elevation = urgent PCI

steps.lead: The two most tested numbers: GRACE **>3%** = angiography within 72 hours (NSTEMI); **120 minutes** = STEMI primary PCI window.

steps.q: Imagine Desmond had presented to a rural hospital where PCI could not happen within 120 minutes. His BP is 150/90 mmHg. What is the next step?
o: Wait for PCI the next morning
steps.r: PCI not possible in time = **fibrinolysis**. BP is below the 180/110 contraindication. Repeat ECG at 60–90 minutes.

steps.title: NSTEMI pathway
nodes: GRACE ≤3%: add ticagrelor (or clopidogrel 300 mg if high bleeding risk)
GRACE >3% or unstable: angiography within 72 hours + second antiplatelet + GTN
Left main, triple vessel or not suitable for PCI: consider CABG

points: Pain settled; HR back to 70 bpm

steps.lead: Discharge: ramipril, bisoprolol, atorvastatin 80 mg, aspirin 75 mg lifelong, prasugrel 12 months. EF 35% + diabetes = add **eplerenone**.

points: Back 3 weeks later: **sharp** chest pain, worse lying flat
ECG: **widespread ST elevation with PR depression**
Asks about driving: 10 days post-angioplasty, feels well

steps.q: He is already on antiplatelets. What is the most appropriate treatment for this new pain?
steps.r: **Dressler's syndrome**. Already on antiplatelets, so **high-dose aspirin for 1–2 weeks**. Not a new occlusion, so no PCI. Driving: 1 week after successful angioplasty.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' for ST elevation vs depression, why troponin is delayed, how a drug in the stem works, or 'Which is the most likely cause of his collapse?' (VF).

steps.lead: Smoking, diabetes and hypertension built the plaque over decades. The rupture in front of the TV was the acute event.

steps.q: Why does Desmond's ECG show ST **elevation**?
o: Previous scar from an old MI
steps.r: Complete occlusion injures the **full thickness** of the wall: ST elevation. Partial occlusion is subendocardial: ST depression or T inversion.

steps.lead: Desmond's RCA was completely blocked, so the inferior wall was injured through its full thickness.

visual.title: Contrast: subendocardial ischaemia (NSTEMI)
visual.caption: ST depression V4–V6 with T-wave inversion in I and aVL, no ST elevation. With a rising troponin this is NSTEMI; with a normal troponin, unstable angina.

steps.text: If the RCA were only **partly** blocked, the injury would stay subendocardial and the ECG would look like this.

steps.lead: Troponin 38 ng/L at under an hour, 2150 ng/L by 3 hours: myocytes had to **die and leak** first.
Every drug hits a step in the flow: antiplatelets stop aggregation, anticoagulants block the cascade, PCI opens the artery, ramipril and bisoprolol limit remodelling.

steps.title: Where each drug acts
head: Drug
Target
Effect
rows: Irreversibly inhibits COX, less thromboxane A2

visual.title: Monitor strip in the cath lab
visual.caption: Chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable QRS complexes: ventricular fibrillation. Shockable rhythm: defibrillate.

steps.lead: He arrested at **reperfusion**: freshly reperfused ischaemic myocardium is electrically unstable, so VF strikes then.

steps.text: Pulseless collapse soon after ACS pain = **ventricular fibrillation**, the commonest cause of death in ACS.
Pulseless collapse is not complete heart block. Heart block (proximal RCA) gives bradycardia and syncope, but a pulse remains.

mcq.q: Which ECG finding with ACS symptoms is treated as a STEMI-equivalent?
mcq.r: New LBBB is always treated the same as a STEMI.

mcq.q: What distinguishes unstable angina from NSTEMI?
o: Troponin is normal in unstable angina
mcq.r: Both can have the same ECG changes; troponin is raised in NSTEMI and normal in unstable angina.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests costochondritis rather than ACS?
o: Tenderness on palpation of the chest wall
mcq.r: Costochondritis is tender to press and hurts on inspiration; treat with NSAIDs or paracetamol.

mcq.q: How soon after presentation should the ECG be done in suspected ACS?
ST elevation in V1–V3 indicates occlusion of which artery?
In NSTEMI, which GRACE score means coronary angiography within 72 hours?
mcq.r: GRACE >3% → angiography within 72 hours of admission.

mcq.q: Which blood pressure contraindicates fibrinolysis in STEMI?
mcq.r: Severe hypertension, systolic >180 or diastolic >110 mmHg, contraindicates fibrinolysis.

mcq.q: How long should a patient avoid driving a car after successful angioplasty for MI?
mcq.r: 1 week, then resume once recovered and the GP confirms it is safe.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of death in ACS?
mcq.r: VF, from electrical instability in ischaemic or reperfused myocardium.

mcq.q: Why does NSTEMI cause ST depression rather than ST elevation?
mcq.r: Incomplete occlusion affects only the subendocardium, giving ST depression or T-wave inversion.

prompts.q: What separates unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: troponin splits angina from infarction; the ECG splits NSTEMI from STEMI.

points.p: Unstable angina: ischaemic pain with a normal troponin
points.why: A normal troponin with ischaemic ECG changes is still unstable angina, not NSTEMI.

points.p: NSTEMI: raised troponin without ST elevation (ST depression, T-wave inversion or normal ECG)
points.why: A normal ECG does not exclude NSTEMI; serial troponins decide.

points.p: STEMI: ST elevation plus raised troponin, full-thickness infarction
points.why: STEMI needs urgent reperfusion, so treatment starts before the troponin returns.

points.p: Usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombus
points.why: Stable angina has no thrombus; the plaque rupture is what makes it acute.

prompts.q: What is the classic presentation of ACS, and who presents atypically?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: an elderly diabetic woman with epigastric pain and breathlessness can still be an MI.

points.p: Central crushing chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw
points.why: Pain lasting over 15 to 20 minutes at rest points to ACS rather than stable angina.

points.p: Sweating, nausea, breathlessness, palpitations or syncope
points.why: Autonomic symptoms are often the clue when the pain is vague.

points.p: Diabetics, women and the elderly can present atypically or silently, without chest pain
points.why: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy blunts pain, so 'silent MI' is a common SBA twist.

points.p: Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, family history
points.why: These also feed the GRACE and secondary prevention questions.

prompts.q: Which ECG leads localise each coronary territory?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the leads, then the artery, then look for reciprocal change.

points.p: Inferior (RCA): ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression I/aVL
points.why: Inferior MI can also show left axis deviation.

points.p: Anterior (LAD): ST elevation V1 to V3 (V4)
points.why: Anterior MI from the LAD carries the largest area at risk.

points.p: Anterolateral: V1 to V3 plus V5/V6
points.why: Lateral extension means V5 and V6 are also involved.

points.p: Lateral (left circumflex): ST elevation I and aVL (V5/V6)
points.why: Circumflex occlusions are the ones most easily missed on a standard ECG.

points.p: Posterior: ST depression V1 to V3, ST elevation V7 to V9
points.why: Tall R waves with ST depression in V1 to V3 should make you record posterior leads.

prompts.q: What ECG findings are treated as a STEMI, and what mimics ACS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: new LBBB means reperfusion; tenderness on palpation means think chest wall.

points.p: New left bundle branch block is treated as a STEMI-equivalent
points.why: A new LBBB with chest pain goes down the primary PCI pathway.

points.p: Costochondritis: tender on palpation, pain on inspiration, treated with NSAIDs or paracetamol
points.why: Reproducible tenderness is the distinguishing feature in the stem.

points.p: Coronary vasospasm, strongly associated with cocaine use
points.why: Ask about cocaine in a young patient with chest pain and ST changes.

points.p: Pericarditis (including Dressler's): widespread saddle ST elevation with PR depression
points.why: Widespread ST elevation across territories plus PR depression is pericarditis, not STEMI.

prompts.q: What are the complications of an MI and their clues?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the timing and the new sign to the complication.

points.p: Ventricular fibrillation, the commonest cause of death in ACS
points.why: VF arises early from electrically unstable ischaemic myocardium.

points.p: Cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure: lung crackles, hypotension
points.why: Crackles on auscultation are a poor prognostic sign.

points.p: Ventricular septal rupture: new pansystolic murmur plus acute heart failure
points.why: Needs urgent echo and surgical repair.

points.p: Dressler's syndrome: pericarditis weeks after MI
points.why: Treat with high-dose aspirin for 1 to 2 weeks.

points.p: Proximal RCA occlusion: bradycardia and complete heart block
points.why: Proximal RCA occlusion carries a 3-fold higher 30-day mortality; manage with urgent PCI.

prompts.q: What are the first investigations in suspected ACS, and how is troponin used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ECG first, troponin repeated, never wait for troponin in a STEMI.

points.p: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival
points.why: The ECG decides whether the patient goes straight to reperfusion.

points.p: Serial high-sensitivity troponins, looking for a rise or fall
points.why: A single raised troponin is not enough; it is the change between samples that confirms MI.

points.p: Troponin takes 2 to 3 hours to rise after the infarct
points.why: An early normal troponin does not exclude MI.

points.p: CK-MB is best for detecting reinfarction
points.why: CK-MB falls faster than troponin, so a fresh rise means new infarction.

points.p: Also FBC, U&Es and chest X-ray
points.why: Anaemia and renal function affect bleeding risk and drug choice.

prompts.q: How is an NSTEMI risk-stratified and what does the result change?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: GRACE number, then the angiography deadline.

points.p: GRACE score estimates 6-month mortality in NSTEMI
points.why: Ischaemic risk scores, not troponin level alone, decide the timing of angiography.

points.p: GRACE above 3% or unstable: coronary angiography (with PCI if needed) within 72 hours
points.why: Haemodynamic instability means immediate angiography regardless of score.

points.p: GRACE 3% or less: medical management with a second antiplatelet
points.why: Clopidogrel 300mg is preferred if bleeding risk is high.

prompts.q: What is the immediate management of suspected ACS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: aspirin first, oxygen only if hypoxic, check BP before GTN.

points.p: Aspirin 300mg orally straight away
points.why: Given before the diagnosis is confirmed.

points.p: Oxygen only if saturations below 94%
points.why: Routine oxygen in non-hypoxic patients is a classic wrong answer.

points.p: GTN, avoided if systolic BP below 90 mmHg
points.why: Nitrates drop preload and can crash an already hypotensive patient, e.g. right ventricular MI.

points.p: IV morphine with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide for severe pain
points.why: Always pair the opioid with an antiemetic.

points.p: Second antiplatelet: prasugrel 60mg if PCI and not anticoagulated, clopidogrel if anticoagulated, ticagrelor otherwise
points.why: Ticagrelor is used with caution over 75 because of bleeding.

points.p: Anticoagulation with fondaparinux or unfractionated heparin
points.why: Heparin is preferred when immediate angiography or PCI is planned.

prompts.q: What is the reperfusion choice in STEMI and its time limits?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: PCI if within 12 hours of onset and deliverable within 120 minutes, otherwise fibrinolysis.

points.p: Primary PCI with drug-eluting stent via the radial artery
points.why: Radial access has fewer bleeding complications than femoral.

points.p: PCI if onset within 12 hours and it can be delivered within 120 minutes
points.why: Both time limits must be met to choose PCI.

points.p: Otherwise fibrinolysis (e.g. alteplase) with fondaparinux
points.why: Severe hypertension (systolic over 180 or diastolic over 110) contraindicates fibrinolysis.

points.p: Repeat ECG at 60 to 90 minutes after fibrinolysis; rescue PCI if ST elevation persists
points.why: Failure to resolve ST elevation by half means failed fibrinolysis.

points.p: CABG for left main or triple vessel disease, or if PCI is unsuitable
points.why: Ongoing pain or instability after PCI may also need CABG.

prompts.q: Which drugs go on the discharge list after an MI, and for how long?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the secondary prevention list, plus the extras for low EF.

points.p: Lifelong aspirin 75mg
points.why: Aspirin drops to 75mg once the loading dose is given.

points.p: Second antiplatelet (ticagrelor or prasugrel) for 12 months
points.why: Clopidogrel is the option if the patient is also anticoagulated.

points.p: ACE inhibitor such as ramipril, started within 24 hours
points.why: ACE inhibitors limit remodelling after infarction.

points.p: Beta-blocker such as bisoprolol
points.why: Beta-blockers reduce oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk.

points.p: High-dose statin: atorvastatin 80mg
points.why: Atorvastatin 80mg regardless of baseline cholesterol.

points.p: Eplerenone if ejection fraction below 40%
points.why: Especially with heart failure or diabetes; DVLA: no driving for 1 week after successful angioplasty.

prompts.q: Why does STEMI show ST elevation but NSTEMI does not?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: complete versus partial occlusion.

points.p: STEMI: complete occlusion causes transmural, full-thickness injury
points.why: Transmural injury currents point towards the overlying leads, giving ST elevation.

points.p: NSTEMI/UA: partial occlusion causes subendocardial ischaemia, giving ST depression or T-wave inversion
points.why: The subendocardium is most vulnerable because it is furthest from the epicardial arteries.

points.p: Troponin rises only once cardiomyocytes are irreversibly damaged, taking 2 to 3 hours
points.why: This is why troponin is normal in unstable angina.

prompts.q: How do the ACS drugs work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the drug to the step it blocks.

points.p: Antiplatelets (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors) stop platelet aggregation and thrombus growth
points.why: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX; clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block the P2Y12 receptor.

points.p: Anticoagulants (fondaparinux, heparin) inhibit the coagulation cascade
points.why: Fondaparinux inhibits factor Xa; heparin potentiates antithrombin.

points.p: PCI mechanically reopens the artery; fibrinolysis dissolves the clot
points.why: Fibrinolytics convert plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin.

points.p: ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers reduce remodelling and myocardial oxygen demand
points.why: This is why they are lifelong after MI.

glossary.ACS: Acute coronary syndrome: unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI caused by a sudden fall in coronary blood flow.
glossary.troponin: A heart muscle protein released into the blood when cardiomyocytes die; the key blood test for myocardial infarction.
glossary.hs-troponin: High-sensitivity troponin assay that detects very small rises, so serial samples hours apart can confirm or exclude MI.
glossary.CK-MB: A heart-specific creatine kinase enzyme that falls quickly after MI, making it useful for spotting reinfarction.
glossary.unstable angina: Ischaemic chest pain at rest or worsening, with normal troponin, so there is no infarction.
glossary.stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion relieved by rest or GTN, caused by fixed narrowing without thrombus.
glossary.crescendo angina: Angina becoming more frequent or severe over a short period, a form of unstable angina.
glossary.NSTEMI: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction: raised troponin without ST elevation, usually from partial coronary occlusion.
glossary.STEMI: ST-elevation myocardial infarction: full-thickness infarction from complete occlusion, needing urgent reperfusion.
glossary.plaque rupture: Tearing of the cap over an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing material that triggers platelet clumping and clot formation.
glossary.atherosclerotic: Describing fatty, fibrous plaques that build up in artery walls and narrow them.
glossary.transmural: Affecting the full thickness of the heart wall, from endocardium to epicardium.
glossary.subendocardial: The inner layer of heart muscle, the first to become ischaemic when blood supply falls.
glossary.reciprocal: ST depression in leads facing the opposite side of the heart to an area of ST elevation, supporting a true STEMI.
glossary.LBBB: Left bundle branch block: delayed conduction in the left ventricle giving broad QRS; new LBBB with chest pain is treated as STEMI.
glossary.RCA: Right coronary artery, supplying the inferior wall and usually the SA and AV nodes.
glossary.LAD: Left anterior descending artery, supplying the anterior wall and most of the septum.
glossary.circumflex: The left circumflex artery, supplying the lateral wall of the left ventricle.
glossary.left axis deviation: The heart's overall electrical axis pointing further left than normal, seen on ECG; can accompany inferior MI.
glossary.complete heart block: No atrial impulses reach the ventricles, causing a slow independent ventricular rhythm; a risk after inferior MI.
glossary.GRACE score: A risk score estimating death after ACS; in NSTEMI a value above 3% means angiography within 72 hours.
glossary.TIMI: A simpler risk score for unstable angina and NSTEMI, predicting death, reinfarction or urgent revascularisation.
glossary.Killip: A bedside classification of heart failure severity after MI, from no crackles (I) to cardiogenic shock (IV).
glossary.PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention: a catheter through the wrist or groin opens the blocked artery with a balloon and stent.
glossary.primary PCI: PCI performed as the first reperfusion treatment for STEMI, without fibrinolysis beforehand.
glossary.drug-eluting stent: A metal coronary stent coated with a drug that slows tissue regrowth, reducing re-narrowing.
glossary.coronary angiography: X-ray imaging of the coronary arteries with injected contrast to find blockages, often followed by PCI.
glossary.fibrinolysis: Clot-dissolving drug treatment for STEMI when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes.
glossary.alteplase: A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clot.
glossary.CABG: Coronary artery bypass graft: open-heart surgery that uses a vein or artery to bypass blocked coronary arteries.
glossary.triple vessel disease: Significant narrowing in all three main coronary arteries, often better treated by CABG than PCI.
glossary.left main: The short left main coronary artery before it splits into the LAD and circumflex; disease here threatens most of the left ventricle.
glossary.MONA: Old mnemonic for immediate ACS care: morphine, oxygen, nitrates, aspirin; oxygen now only if saturations below 94%.
glossary.GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate, a nitrate that dilates veins and coronary arteries to relieve ischaemic pain; avoid if systolic BP under 90.
glossary.metoclopramide: An antiemetic given with morphine to stop opioid-induced nausea and vomiting.
glossary.prasugrel: A P2Y12 antiplatelet given with aspirin before PCI in patients not on an anticoagulant.
glossary.ticagrelor: A P2Y12 antiplatelet used with aspirin in ACS, given with caution over 75 because of bleeding risk.
glossary.clopidogrel: A P2Y12 antiplatelet used with aspirin when bleeding risk is high or the patient is already anticoagulated.
glossary.P2Y12: A platelet ADP receptor; blocking it with clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor stops platelets clumping.
glossary.DAPT: Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually continued for 12 months after ACS.
glossary.fondaparinux: An injectable factor Xa inhibitor used as anticoagulation in ACS and alongside fibrinolysis.
glossary.unfractionated heparin: An anticoagulant given IV that boosts antithrombin; preferred when immediate PCI is planned as it is quickly reversible.
glossary.ramipril: An ACE inhibitor started within 24 hours of MI to limit ventricular remodelling.
glossary.bisoprolol: A cardioselective beta-blocker that slows the heart and lowers oxygen demand after MI.
glossary.atorvastatin: A statin given at 80mg after ACS to lower cholesterol and stabilise plaques.
glossary.eplerenone: An aldosterone antagonist added after MI when ejection fraction is below 40%.
glossary.ejection fraction: The percentage of blood the left ventricle pumps out per beat; below 40% means significant systolic dysfunction.
glossary.remodelling: Harmful changes in ventricular size and shape after MI that lead to heart failure.
glossary.cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion because the heart is failing as a pump.
glossary.ventricular septal rupture: A tear in the wall between the ventricles days after MI, causing a new pansystolic murmur and heart failure.
glossary.pansystolic murmur: A murmur lasting through the whole of systole, heard with septal rupture or mitral regurgitation.
glossary.ventricular fibrillation: Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no output, the commonest cause of death early in ACS.
glossary.Dressler's syndrome: Autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI, with chest pain, fever and widespread ST elevation.
glossary.pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium causing sharp pleuritic chest pain eased by sitting forward, with saddle ST elevation.
glossary.PR depression: Downward shift of the PR segment on ECG, a typical sign of pericarditis.
glossary.costochondritis: Inflammation of the rib cartilage causing chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall.
glossary.vasospasm: Sudden tightening of a coronary artery causing ischaemia, classically triggered by cocaine.
glossary.silent MI: A myocardial infarction without typical chest pain, more common in diabetics, women and the elderly.
glossary.DVLA: The UK driving licence agency; after successful angioplasty for ACS the patient should not drive for 1 week.

technique.stem:
A 71 year old woman has had nausea and breathlessness for 3 hours. She has no chest pain. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension.

Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

Her ECG shows ST depression in leads V4–V6.

Investigations:
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis. In a breathless diabetic with ECG changes and two troponins, the examiner wants you to place her on the ACS spectrum.
Diabetics and women can present **atypically** without chest pain. ST depression (not elevation) means partial occlusion. A **rising** troponin from 64 to 412 means myocyte death.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infarction (raised, rising troponin) without ST elevation = **NSTEMI**.

elim: Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation and PR depression, and pain that changes with posture.
PE is possible in a breathless patient, but ST depression in a coronary territory with a steep troponin rise points to ACS.
There is no ST elevation and no new LBBB, so it is not a STEMI.
Unstable angina has the same ECG changes but a **normal** troponin.

steps.x: B. Rule: ST elevation decides STEMI vs not; troponin decides NSTEMI vs unstable angina. No chest pain in a diabetic woman does not exclude ACS.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST depression in V4–V6, no ST elevation.

technique.stem:
A 59 year old man has had central chest tightness for 1 hour. It started while he was walking his dog. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day.

His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 148/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.

His ECG shows ST depression in leads V4–V6. He has been given aspirin 300 mg.

Investigations:
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: 'Next investigation' means the ECG and first bloods are already done. What do you still need to make the diagnosis?
Pain began only **1 hour** ago and the troponin of 9 ng/L is normal. Troponin does not rise until **2–3 hours** after MI, so a normal first value cannot rule out NSTEMI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Repeat the troponin to look for a rising or falling trend: **serial troponins**.

elim: A CXR is an initial test but does not tell you whether he is having an MI.
CT coronary angiography is for stable chest pain, not an ongoing possible ACS.
Exercise testing in a possible ACS is dangerous and not a diagnostic step here.
Echo can show wall motion abnormality but does not define NSTEMI vs unstable angina.

steps.x: D. Rule: early normal troponin = repeat it. NSTEMI vs unstable angina is decided by troponin, and troponin needs 2–3 hours.

technique.stem:
A 64 year old man has central crushing chest pain associated with sweating and nausea for 40 minutes.

His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.

His ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1–V4. The hospital has an on-site catheter laboratory.

He is treated with aspirin, prasugrel, intravenous morphine and glyceryl trinitrate.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: 'Next step' after a list of drugs: the examiner has given the immediate medical treatment, so they want the **reperfusion** decision.
Anterior STEMI, within 12 hours of onset, and PCI is clearly deliverable within 120 minutes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: STEMI + PCI available in time = **primary PCI**.

elim: Fibrinolysis is only for when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes.
GRACE stratifies NSTEMI, not STEMI.
CABG is for left main / triple vessel disease, failure of PCI or unsuitability for PCI, not first-line STEMI.
Never wait for troponin in STEMI; the ECG has made the diagnosis.

steps.x: D. Rule: STEMI within 12 hours and PCI within 120 minutes = primary PCI; otherwise fibrinolysis.

technique.stem:
A 55 year old man has had central crushing chest pain for 2 hours. He has no history of heart disease and does not use recreational drugs.

His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

His ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1–V4 with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the ECG changes?
o: Complete coronary occlusion causing transmural injury
Partial coronary occlusion causing subendocardial ischaemia

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the finding (ST elevation), not name the disease.
Territorial elevation with reciprocal change = acute STEMI. No old MI, no cocaine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ST elevation reflects **transmural**, full-thickness injury from **complete occlusion**.

elim: Vasospasm is linked to cocaine use, which he denies.
Pericarditis gives widespread elevation without reciprocal depression.
Partial occlusion gives ST depression or T inversion (NSTEMI / UA).
An aneurysm causes persistent elevation weeks after an old MI; he has no cardiac history.

steps.x: A. Rule: complete occlusion = transmural = ST elevation; partial occlusion = subendocardial = ST depression.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression.

practice.stem:
A 27 year old man has central chest pain that started while he was dancing at a party. He used cocaine 1 hour earlier. He has no past medical history.

His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.

His ECG shows transient ST elevation in leads V2–V4, which resolves after sublingual glyceryl trinitrate. There is no chest wall tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his chest pain?
practice.e: Young man, **cocaine**, transient ST elevation that resolves with GTN = **cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm**. Plaque rupture needs risk factors; pericarditis gives widespread, persistent elevation.

steps.x: It asks for a **cause**, not a label. Think: what made this artery stop flowing?
Young, no history, cocaine. ST elevation that **goes away with GTN** = spasm, not a fixed clot.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm.**

elim: No tearing pain to the back, no arm BP difference.
27 with no risk factors; a clot would not vanish with GTN.
No chest wall tenderness.
Pericarditis: widespread, persistent elevation, not transient territorial V2–V4.

steps.x: C. Rule: young + cocaine + chest pain = **coronary vasospasm** until proven otherwise.

practice.stem:
A 68 year old man was admitted 3 days ago with an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI. He now has sudden worsening breathlessness.

His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.

There is a new loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a palpable thrill, and crackles at both lung bases.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: New **pansystolic murmur + acute heart failure** days after MI = **ventricular septal rupture**: urgent echo and surgical repair. Dressler's is weeks later with pericarditic pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis, in a patient **3 days** after a STEMI. Think complications by timing.

clues: 3 days ago with an anterior STEMI
new loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge
steps.x: Days post-MI + new pansystolic murmur + heart failure + low BP = mechanical complication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ventricular septal rupture.**

elim: Ejection systolic murmur, not a sudden new pansystolic one.
Weeks after MI, with pericarditic pain and widespread ST elevation.
No fever or embolic signs; murmur is too sudden.
Aneurysm is later, with persistent ST elevation, not a new thrill.

steps.x: E. Rule: **days** post-MI + new pansystolic murmur + acute heart failure = VSR. Urgent echo.

practice.stem:
A 60 year old woman had a myocardial infarction 4 weeks ago. She now has sharp central chest pain that is worse on lying flat and a low-grade fever.

Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.

Her ECG shows widespread ST elevation with PR depression. There is no reciprocal ST depression.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: **Widespread ST elevation + PR depression** weeks after MI = **Dressler's syndrome**. Re-infarction is territorial with reciprocal depression.

steps.x: Diagnosis, **4 weeks** after an MI. Timing points to a late complication.

clues: widespread ST elevation with PR depression
steps.x: Positional pain + fever + widespread ST elevation with PR depression = pericardial inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-infarction pericarditis: **Dressler's syndrome.**

elim: Pain is positional, not tender on palpation; ECG is abnormal.
PE gives hypoxia and tachypnoea; sats are 97%.
Re-infarction is territorial with reciprocal depression.
VSR occurs days after MI with a new pansystolic murmur.

steps.x: B. Rule: **weeks** post-MI + widespread ST elevation + PR depression = Dressler's.

practice.stem:
A 57 year old man has central crushing chest pain associated with sweating for 30 minutes. He smokes and has hypertension.

His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 46 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

An ECG is recorded (see item resources).
practice.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
practice.e: ST elevation **II, III, aVF** with reciprocal I/aVL depression = inferior MI = **RCA**. Bradycardia fits a proximal RCA. V1–V3 = LAD; I and aVL alone = circumflex.

steps.x: It asks for the **artery**. Read the ECG leads, map to a wall, then to a vessel.
ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF; reciprocal depression I, aVL. Bradycardia hints the SA/AV node supply is hit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inferior STEMI = **right coronary artery**.

elim: Circumflex: ST elevation in I and aVL, which here are depressed.
Diagonal branch: high lateral changes, not inferior.
LAD: ST elevation V1–V3; chest leads are normal.
Left main: widespread depression with aVR elevation and shock.

steps.x: E. Rule: **II, III, aVF = RCA**. Add bradycardia = proximal RCA, watch for heart block.

practice.stem:
A 63 year old man has central crushing chest pain with sweating for 1 hour. He has type 2 diabetes and smokes.

His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

His 12-lead ECG shows horizontal ST depression in leads V1–V3. Posterior leads show ST elevation in V7–V9.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: ST depression **V1–V3** with ST elevation **V7–V9** = **posterior STEMI**: the anterior leads see the posterior wall in reverse. Calling it NSTEMI delays reperfusion.

steps.x: Diagnosis: place him on the ACS spectrum and name the territory.

clues: central crushing chest pain with sweating
steps.x: ACS story. V1–V3 depression is the **mirror image** of posterior elevation; V7–V9 confirm it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Posterior STEMI** (needs reperfusion).

elim: Anterior STEMI = ST elevation V1–V3, not depression.
Inferior STEMI = elevation II, III, aVF; not mentioned.
The trap: V1–V3 depression looks like NSTEMI, but V7–V9 elevation makes it a STEMI.
Troponin is raised, so it is infarction, not unstable angina.

steps.x: D. Rule: ST depression V1–V3 in an ACS story = **check V7–V9** for posterior STEMI.

practice.stem:
A 69 year old woman has had three episodes of central chest tightness in the past 2 days, the latest at rest this morning lasting 15 minutes. Over the previous month her exertional chest pain had become more frequent. She is now pain free.

Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.

Her ECG shows T-wave inversion in leads V4–V6.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Crescendo angina, now **at rest**, ischaemic ECG, **normal serial troponins** = **unstable angina**. A rising troponin would make it NSTEMI.

steps.x: Diagnosis. Place her on the ACS spectrum using ECG and troponin.

clues: the latest at rest this morning
exertional chest pain had become more frequent
steps.x: Crescendo pattern + rest pain = unstable plaque. Both troponins (8, 9 ng/L) are **normal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ACS without infarction: **unstable angina.**

elim: No chest wall tenderness; ECG is ischaemic.
NSTEMI needs a raised troponin; hers is normal twice.
Stable angina is predictable and exertional, not at rest.
No ST elevation.

steps.x: E. Rule: ACS story + **normal serial troponin** = unstable angina; raised = NSTEMI.

practice.stem:
A 66 year old woman has had intermittent central chest pain at rest for 6 hours. She has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. She is now pain free.

Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.

Her ECG shows T-wave inversion in leads V3–V6. She has been given aspirin 300 mg. Her calculated GRACE score is 6.2%.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Rising troponin, no ST elevation = **NSTEMI**. GRACE **>3%** = coronary angiography within 72 hours. CTCA, exercise ECG and perfusion scans are for stable chest pain.

steps.x: Next **investigation**. First decide which ACS this is, then apply the rule.
Troponin 88 → 346 ng/L: rising, so infarction. No ST elevation = NSTEMI. GRACE above 3%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NSTEMI + GRACE >3% = **coronary angiography within 72 hours.**

elim: CT coronary angiography is for stable chest pain.
Exercise testing is unsafe and unhelpful in confirmed NSTEMI.
Perfusion scans assess stable disease.
Echo is useful later for LV function, but does not treat the culprit.

steps.x: A. Rule: NSTEMI, GRACE **>3%** → angiography within **72 hours**.

practice.stem:
A 70 year old man was admitted 5 days ago with an NSTEMI. He now has a new episode of central chest pain lasting 30 minutes.

His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.

His troponin has remained elevated since admission.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test to detect reinfarction?
practice.e: Troponin stays raised for days, so it misses a second event. **CK-MB** falls quickly, so re-elevation = **reinfarction**. BNP reflects heart failure.

steps.x: It asks for a **blood test** to detect reinfarction.

clues: admitted 5 days ago with an NSTEMI
new episode of central chest pain
troponin has remained elevated since admission
steps.x: Troponin is already high, so a new rise is hard to see. You need a marker that clears fast.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CK-MB.**

elim: BNP reflects heart failure, not new infarction.
CRP is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
D-dimer is for PE/DVT; not specific to MI.
Troponin is still raised from the first MI.

steps.x: C. Rule: reinfarction within days = **CK-MB**, because troponin stays high.

practice.stem:
A 73 year old woman has central crushing chest pain for 1 hour. She has atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban.

Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 96 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

Her ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. She has been given aspirin 300 mg and is going for primary PCI.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate second antiplatelet?
practice.e: Already **anticoagulated** (apixaban), so the second antiplatelet is **clopidogrel**. Prasugrel is for PCI only when not anticoagulated.

steps.x: Pick the **second antiplatelet**. The choice depends on PCI and anticoagulation.

clues: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF
steps.x: Inferior STEMI going for PCI, but **already anticoagulated**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anticoagulated = **clopidogrel.**

elim: Abciximab (GP IIb/IIIa) is not the standard second antiplatelet in the notes.
Dipyridamole is not used in ACS.
Prasugrel only if **not** anticoagulated; bleeding risk.
Ticagrelor + apixaban + aspirin: too much bleeding risk.

steps.x: B. Rule: on apixaban or warfarin = **clopidogrel**; PCI and not anticoagulated = prasugrel.

practice.stem:
A 61 year old man has central crushing chest pain with sweating for 2 hours. He is at a district hospital where the nearest primary PCI centre cannot treat him within 120 minutes.

His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

His ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1–V4. He has been given aspirin 300 mg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Observe and repeat troponin at 3 hours
Transfer for primary PCI the next morning
practice.e: STEMI within 12 hours, PCI **not possible within 120 minutes** = **fibrinolysis** (alteplase + fondaparinux). BP is below 180/110. Repeat ECG at 60–90 minutes.

steps.x: Next **management** step in a STEMI. Ask: can PCI happen within 120 minutes?
Anterior STEMI, within 12 hours, PCI not timely, no BP contraindication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fibrinolysis with alteplase.**

elim: CABG is for left main or triple vessel disease, not first reperfusion.
Heparin alone does not reperfuse the artery.
Never wait for troponin in STEMI.
Delaying reperfusion overnight loses myocardium.

steps.x: B. Rule: PCI not within **120 minutes** = fibrinolysis, unless BP >180/110.

practice.stem:
A 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes is being discharged 5 days after an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI. He is taking aspirin 75 mg, ticagrelor, ramipril, bisoprolol and atorvastatin 80 mg.

His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.

An echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%.
practice.q: Which additional drug is most appropriate?
practice.e: Post-MI with **EF <40%**, especially with diabetes, add **eplerenone**. Potassium is normal, so it is safe. The others are not standard secondary prevention.

steps.x: Which **extra drug** at discharge after a STEMI. Check what he already takes.

clues: aspirin 75 mg, ticagrelor, ramipril, bisoprolol and atorvastatin 80 mg
steps.x: Full secondary prevention already. EF below 40% + diabetes. Potassium 4.4 is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add an aldosterone antagonist: **eplerenone.**

elim: Amlodipine is for BP; not post-MI prognosis.
Digoxin is for AF rate control; no AF here.
Ivabradine is not standard post-MI prevention.
Nicorandil is for angina symptoms; he is pain free.

steps.x: C. Rule: post-MI + **EF <40%** (esp. diabetes) = add eplerenone.

practice.stem:
A 65 year old woman has central crushing chest pain with sweating that began 1 hour ago. She has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. She has had no treatment yet apart from aspirin.

Her ECG shows ST depression in leads V4–V6.

Investigations:
labs: High-sensitivity troponin T (1 hour after onset)
High-sensitivity troponin T (4 hours after onset)
practice.q: Which best explains the normal first troponin result?
o: Coronary reperfusion is required before troponin is released
Ischaemia must last over 24 hours before any myocyte dies
Renal clearance of troponin is fastest in the first hours
Time is needed for myocyte necrosis and leakage into the circulation
Troponin is released only after platelet degranulation
practice.e: Troponin leaks only from **irreversibly damaged cardiomyocytes**. The 2–3 hour delay is time for necrosis and leakage, hence serial troponins. No reperfusion was needed for it to rise.

steps.x: **Mechanism**: why is the first troponin normal in a real NSTEMI?

clues: no treatment yet apart from aspirin
steps.x: Sample at 1 hour normal, at 4 hours 520 ng/L. It rose with no reperfusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Myocytes must **die and leak** before troponin appears: about 2–3 hours.

elim: It rose without any reperfusion.
Troponin rises within 2–3 hours, not after 24.
Renal clearance does not explain a delayed rise.
Platelets do not release troponin; myocytes do.

steps.x: D. Rule: troponin = **myocyte necrosis**, rises 2–3 hours after onset, so repeat it.
